candidates.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
candidates.proposition: Defining God beyond space and time and using God to fill explanatory gaps creates an unconstrained just-so story rather than warranted knowledge.
candidates.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted first-person skeptical argument is delivered during Matt Dillahunty's opening statement.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move states the central skeptical objection that the God hypothesis lacks discriminatory explanatory power and should not replace acknowledged uncertainty.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Matthew Adelstein's use of a transcendent divine mind to explain otherwise improbable features of reality.

candidates.contextSummary: After illustrating the limits of statistical inference with dice, Dillahunty argues that a hidden, transcendent God can explain anything and therefore warrants nothing without better evidence.

candidates.speaker: Matthew Adelstein
candidates.proposition: The cited facts about existence, consciousness, life-permitting laws, and fine-tuned constants are empirical evidence, while universal empiricism is unnecessary and self-defeating.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly introduces Matthew's rebuttal, and Matthew directly addresses Matt by name throughout the move.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move defends the evidential status of the pro case and challenges the epistemic standard that the con side allegedly applies to belief in God.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Matt Dillahunty's demand for sufficient empirical warrant and his contention that the pro case does not provide it.

candidates.contextSummary: At the start of his rebuttal, Adelstein says Dillahunty supplied no contrary evidence, identifies his own evidence as empirical, and argues that requiring empirical support for every justified belief is untenable.

candidates.speaker: Matthew Adelstein
candidates.proposition: A limitless, perfect divine mind is less arbitrary, more parsimonious, and more predictive of life and consciousness than a merely powerful but limited deity.
candidates.attributionBasis: Matthew continues his timed rebuttal in a single sustained response to Matt's challenge about maximal divine attributes.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This move supplies the pro side's main bridge from evidence for some powerful cause to the motion's all-powerful and morally perfect being.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Matt Dillahunty's objection that evidence could at most support a very powerful being rather than an omnimax God.

candidates.contextSummary: Adelstein invokes parsimony, the predictive value of perfection, and the theoretical defect of arbitrary limits to argue that an unlimited mind is preferable to a finitely powerful deity.

candidates.speaker: Matthew Adelstein
candidates.proposition: Statistical likelihood can support belief when prior probabilities are included, and explanatory inference is preferable to stopping at an undifferentiated claim of ignorance.
candidates.attributionBasis: The move remains within Matthew's rebuttal and explicitly identifies Matt's statistical and uncertainty objections before answering them.
candidates.loadBearingReason: It directly defends the probabilistic explanatory method underlying the pro case against the con side's principal methodological criticism.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Matt Dillahunty's claims that statistical likelihood does not establish truth and that uncertainty should remain an open 'I don't know.'

candidates.contextSummary: Adelstein argues that likelihood is evidential once priors are considered and compares inference to God with scientific acceptance of explanatory hypotheses such as dark matter.

candidates.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
candidates.proposition: An observed low-probability arrangement does not by itself justify inferring intentional arrangement, because individual outcomes cannot reveal their generating history without further information.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Matt's rebuttal, and the sustained cards, Galton-board, and dice argument is delivered in his established voice.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is the con side's principal methodological attack on the probabilistic inference from an apparently unlikely universe to intentional divine creation.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Matthew Adelstein's contention that statistically favored explanations and prior probabilities warrant inferring God from observed features.

candidates.contextSummary: Dillahunty uses shuffled cards, individual paths on a Galton board, and dice to distinguish an outcome's probability under intention from evidence that intention actually caused that outcome.

candidates.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
candidates.proposition: A primordial message in every human language would differ from fine-tuning because language is a later human invention, whereas life adapts to the universe it inhabits.
candidates.attributionBasis: Matt answers Matthew's explicit fine-tuning comparison in the open discussion, with the alternating dialogue fixing attribution clearly.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The distinction challenges the proposed analogy meant to make cosmic fine-tuning as evidentially explicit as a deliberately authored message.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Matthew Adelstein's analogy between fine-tuned constants and initial conditions spelling a divine message in every language.

candidates.contextSummary: Dillahunty says a timeless linguistic inscription would uniquely anticipate later human conventions, while observed organisms may simply be the forms able to evolve under existing physical conditions.

candidates.speaker: Matthew Adelstein
candidates.proposition: The cosmological constant occupies an extraordinarily narrow life-permitting range, outside which complex structures would be destroyed almost immediately.
candidates.attributionBasis: Matthew resumes after resolving conversational delay and presents a specific quantitative fine-tuning example before posing a question to Matt.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move provides the concrete physical example supporting the pro side's claim that life-permitting conditions are highly improbable and evidentially significant.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Matt Dillahunty's suggestion that different constants might permit different forms of life adapted to another universe.

candidates.contextSummary: Adelstein focuses on the cosmological constant, claiming that slightly weaker or stronger values would cause rapid collapse or dispersal and that viable values occupy a minute range.

candidates.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
candidates.proposition: Even if only one generated universe permits observers, their presence in that universe does not show that its life-permitting conditions were intentionally created.
candidates.attributionBasis: Matt directly answers Matthew's question and develops a continuous multiverse and observer-selection response until Matthew resumes speaking.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This move supplies the con side's observer-selection alternative to design and denies that extreme life-permitting rarity entails intentional creation.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Matthew Adelstein's claim that the narrow life-permitting range of the cosmological constant supports deliberate fine-tuning.

candidates.contextSummary: Dillahunty disclaims expertise and uncertainty about alternative constants, then argues that even a universe generator producing mostly failures would leave observers only in a viable universe.

candidates.speaker: Matthew Adelstein
candidates.proposition: Observer selection does not erase evidence from survival under improbable conditions, just as surviving a hundred-person firing squad would still support a conspiracy hypothesis.
candidates.attributionBasis: Matthew explicitly turns to Matt's earlier observer-selection claim and presents connected contraception and firing-squad analogies in one turn.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move is the pro side's principal rebuttal to the anthropic objection and seeks to preserve fine-tuning as evidence despite observation being survival-dependent.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Matt Dillahunty's argument that observers could only find themselves in a universe capable of producing observers.

candidates.contextSummary: Adelstein argues that inability to observe one's own nonexistence does not neutralize relevant evidence, illustrating the point with birth despite contraception and survival after mass gunfire.

candidates.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
candidates.proposition: The fact that an observation is more probable if a hypothesis is true does not by itself make that hypothesis more probable as the actual explanation.
candidates.attributionBasis: The alternating exchange makes the speaker boundary clear, and Matt states the probability objection immediately before Matthew contradicts it.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This concise move isolates the core disagreement over whether likelihood comparison licenses updating toward divine intention as the cause of the observed universe.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Matthew Adelstein's claim that observing double sixes is evidence they were intentionally placed and that the same logic supports God.

candidates.contextSummary: During the culminating probability dispute, Dillahunty accuses Adelstein of reversing the conditional relationship between a hypothesis and the likelihood of an observation.
